chunks.text: Bambusa ventricosa McClure, commonly called Buddha belly bamboo or Buddha bamboo, is a bamboo species in the grass family Poaceae, native to Vietnam and to Guangdong province in southern China, first formally described by the American-trained botanist Floyd Alonzo McClure in the Lingnan Science Journal in 1938; its older synonym is Leleba ventricosa. Despite being one of the most recognisable and widely traded ornamental bamboos in the world, its English Wikipedia entry remains a stub with relatively little detail, noting only that it is grown for its 'bulbous and ornamental stems' and that it is a popular subject for bonsai cultivation — a telling gap that underscores how much of the detailed horticultural knowledge about this species currently lives on nursery and botanical-garden websites rather than in general encyclopaedic references. Its Chinese name, 佛肚竹 (fó dù zhú), translates directly as 'Buddha belly bamboo', matching the English common name and reflecting the same visual association with the rounded belly of a Budai/Buddha figure.

This specialist bamboo nursery's profile fills in the horticultural detail that general encyclopaedic sources lack: the plant's signature feature — short, swollen, pot-bellied internodes near the base of the culm — is not a fixed, permanent trait of the species but a stress response, appearing most strongly when the bamboo is grown in a container or deliberately kept somewhat pot-bound and under-watered; a plant grown in open, rich, well-watered ground will often revert to producing mostly normal, straight, unswollen culms. Even under stress-inducing container conditions, growers report that typically only around half of the new shoots in a clump develop the dramatic swollen 'belly' form, with the remainder coming up straight, which means a single clump of Buddha belly bamboo can show both forms side by side. The lower portions of the culm, where the swelling occurs, are usually free of side branches, which is precisely what keeps the bulging internodes visible and ornamental rather than hidden behind foliage. The species typically reaches 6-10 m when allowed to grow freely, does flower occasionally (an unusual trait among ornamental bamboos commonly kept as clipped container specimens) but does not reliably set viable fruit, and has produced at least one popular golden-culmed cultivar, 'Kimmei', with yellow stems striped in green. The source also flags a common point of market confusion: an unrelated, separately named 'Giant Buddha's Belly' sold under the cultivar name Bambusa vulgaris 'Wamin' is a different, shorter plant (around 3-5 m), so buyers and identifiers should check the full species/cultivar name rather than relying on the 'Buddha belly' nickname alone.
